title: “All I Want Is for the War to End”: Displacement Behind the Front Lines in Yemen
author: Carolina Pedrazzi

TAIZ, Yemen*--This week, as Ansarallah forces advanced by the hour to seize
the port city of Mokha and secure access to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait
off the coast of Yemen, residents of Taiz braced for more fighting.

Over the past week, some of the fiercest battles between Ansarallah (also
known as the Houthis) and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces took place in
the hills surrounding Taiz--a crucial trade hub in southwestern Yemen,
situated between Ibb, Mokha, Hodeidah, and Aden.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia bombed five Yemeni governorates more than 50 times
in a single 12-hour span. On Sunday, powerful explosions shook Taiz and
several residential areas were shelled. The Yemeni government attributed the
explosions to Ansarallah. Ansarallah neither claimed the bombings nor denied
them, but the fighting proved decisive ahead of Ansarallah's capture of Mokha
later in the week.

Thousands of households from across the Taiz governorate have been displaced
since September 3, when a new round of intensified fighting began. Across
Yemen, nearly 20,000 have fled their homes, according to the International
Organization for Migration. Over the past week, at least 500 have been killed,
according to the AFP, most of them combatants. Among the dead and wounded are
civilians, including numerous children.

Many of the displaced are from Jabal Habashi, a district in the Taiz
governorate characterized by greenery, agriculture, and terraced hills. Jabal
Habashi has seen the majority of the violence in the area--and its families
have experienced among the highest rates of displacement. Because of its
strategic position, wedged between Taiz and Mokha, it is a crucial passageway
for securing Yemen's west coast.

Yet, as Ansarallah has been increasingly taking hold of the districts
surrounding the provincial capital, which is thus far still under the control
of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, has attempted to retain a sense of
normalcy: Its markets are bustling and people walk the streets, despite the
presence of military convoys bringing in injured fighters to its hospitals.

"When I heard the explosions I remembered the difficult days of the beginning
of the war in 2015," said Taiz city resident Mohammed Abdulmalik, "and felt
with the suffering of the population who witness it nowadays in west Taiz."

## **Civilian Targeting**

Drop Site News visited several hospitals in the city of Taiz, including Al
Thawra and Al Safwah, speaking with local patients hospitalized with injuries
incurred in the ongoing fighting. The aisles of these hospitals were
overflowing with patients; the majority of them were injured fighters,
although the hospital is treating civilians as well. Ashraf, a 47-year-old
construction worker from the Jabal Habashi district, was injured while
attempting to flee his village on Saturday with his family, a day after heavy
fighting with shelling broke out around him. (Ashraf is a pseudonym used for
his safety.)

"We were moving in small separate groups to reduce the risk of being targeted,
and an explosion went off. I lost consciousness and fainted, and was later
evacuated to Taiz."

Ashraf woke up in a hospital surrounded by other wounded civilians, including
children. Still sitting in a hospital bed, he told Drop Site, "It is always us
civilians who suffer the brunt of this war."

At a private hospital also in Taiz, four injured children were in hospital
beds, staying in the same room: three boys and one girl, who was the eldest.
The girl and two of the boys were siblings, while the fourth boy was their
neighbor.

The children's guardian, their uncle, told Drop Site he had brought them from
the Jabal Habashi district to Taiz city after their home was shelled.

"On Friday, we all stayed home because the fighting was fierce," he told us.
"But by the afternoon, things had calmed down, and the children went out to
play in front of the house as usual. Then we heard an explosion nearby and the
screams of other children. We ran out and found the four of them on the floor,
bleeding." He was uncertain whether Ansarallah or the Saudi-backed government
forces had caused the explosion, as both had been firing at each other.

The uncle said they normally could not afford hospital costs, but an
international NGO operating locally funded their stay at the private
facility."I just hope they recover and can return home. Their parents are
stuck in the village, as leaving is too dangerous right now. So I am taking
care of them for the time being."

## **Families Torn Apart**

The Jabal Zaid camp for Internally Displaced People (IDP), nestled between the
green valleys of Taiz governorate, is one of several camps that have absorbed
at least 5,600 households displaced across the Taiz and Hodeidah governorates
in the past week, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination
of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Residents here live in makeshift tents built
from scant, hard-to-source materials.

Rahma, a displaced woman at Jabal Zaid who asked to go only by her first name,
told Drop Site News that her family--who was already displaced by fighting a
decade ago and living in a different IDP camp--had not only been displaced
again, but divided. "When fighting broke out near our [first] camp on Friday,
we took our children and fled the area," she said. "Later that same day, my
husband returned to bring our belongings. We waited for him until the next
day, but he didn't come back. We were terrified he might have been killed or
injured."

Rahma later learned from neighbors that he was stuck in the middle of the
fighting and no one was allowed to leave the area. Five days later, Rahma's
husband was still trapped in the middle of the fighting.

Nujud Mohammed, 28, a mother of six also displaced at Jabal Zaid, described a
similar rupture. She is originally from Al Barah, a site that has seen heavy
clashes due to its position on the supply route connecting Taiz and Mokha, and
has been increasingly targeted by Yemeni government forces and allied
warplanes attempting to repel Ansarallah's advance.

"I tried to return to retrieve our belongings," she said, "but the road was
blocked. We weren't allowed to reach our old camp to take anything. Our area
is now encircled by fighting, and no one can enter or leave. So I returned
with nothing. I praise Allah that we are safe, and I trust that He will
compensate us for everything we lost."

For many at Jabal Zaid, the past week is not a first displacement but a
second, or third. Nujud's family fled to Jabal Habashi nine years ago, at the
start of Yemen's civil war, and had lived there ever since.

"Nine years ago we fled because of the fighting in our area. We spent nine
years in Jabal Habashi, but on Friday, sudden fighting reached our camp. I
immediately took my children and walked from the afternoon until sunset, when
we finally found a car that brought us to this camp."

Surrounded by her children, the youngest of whom is still a toddler, she
cooked flatbread over a fire using plastic basins and a makeshift fire. "It
isn't easy to start over in a new camp, but we have been forced to do so
because we have no alternative."

## **Camp Without Aid**

Nujud and her children now share a single tent with three other families,
relying on the goodwill of their new neighbors for food, mattresses, and other
basic goods. "No humanitarian organizations have arrived yet," she said. "Only
two representatives from a relief agency came to take our names and ask
questions, but no aid has been delivered. We are in dire need of shelter and
food."

Looking at the temporary tent housing her, she said: "All I want at this
moment is for the war to end so I can return."

Mohammed Ahmed, 35, a father in the camp, said his family had expected help to
be awaiting them once they reached safety: "We assumed that as soon as we
reached a safe area, we would receive support from humanitarian organizations,
since we know they cannot reach dangerous frontlines," where their home is.
Indeed, many families chose Jabal Zaid precisely because it is considered a
safe area, yet no agency has provided aid there so far.

"If this situation continues, our children could starve to death, as there are
no job opportunities here and no one to help us."

Fawzi Al-Habashi, Director of the Better Life Association for Coexistence and
Development, a local humanitarian organization that provides food, shelter,
and hygiene assistance, said NGOs "have monitored and documented the
displacement movement, conducted initial needs assessments, and coordinated
with local authorities, providing limited emergency aid to the most vulnerable
families based on priority."

However, as explained by Baraa Shaiban, a Yemeni political analyst who spoke
to Drop Site, the suddenness of the displacement, combined with severe funding
shortages that have characterized many areas of Yemen (particularly areas
controlled by Ansarallah where international aid access has been restricted
for years), has hindered the delivery of emergency assistance.

The Saudi-led war against Ansarallah that began in 2015 after the group took
over Sana'a spawned one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and left over
150,000 dead until an uneasy truce was reached in 2022. Many Yemeni civilians
are experiencing the clashes as a return to heightened instability, as they
see their lives starting over once again, in yet another displacement camp.

As Shaiban put it: "Whatever normality people were hoping to get, it is
quickly fading away."

_* A journalist in Yemen contributed reporting._
